title: Bad Gyal, Luísa Sonza, Milo J & More: Best Quotes From Billboard Brasil and Billboard Español’s 2026 Latin Grammys Activation
summary: During a two-day event presented by Meta at Las Vegas' Museum of Illusions, Latin music stars opened up about their personal journeys.
contentText:
Ahead of the 27th Annual Latin Grammy Awards, Billboard Brasil and Billboard Español teamed up with Meta for a two-day activation at the Museum of Illusions in Las Vegas on Nov. 10–11. The immersive experience brought artists and nominees into a world of mind-bending exhibits, where they tried on Meta’s smart glasses, explored optical illusions and stepped in front of the camera for candid conversations about their music, careers and more.

From personal revelations and unexpected anecdotes to reflections on creative breakthroughs, the artists had plenty to share. Here are 15 of the most memorable quotes from the experience.

Luísa Sonza on her breakthrough beyond Brazil

For Brazilian pop star Luísa Sonza, earning her first Latin Grammy nomination outside the Brazilian categories — best reggaetón performance for “Uñas afiladas” with Sofía Reyes —  was an unexpected milestone. “The nomination was a surprise to me. I didn’t think it would happen,” she said, describing the recognition as “something very beautiful, an achievement.”

What made the moment even more meaningful was sharing it with an artist she considers a friend. Sonza recalled how their collaboration came together organically, without awards or commercial expectations in mind: “We didn’t make the songs thinking about anything else, just because we liked each other.” Their creative chemistry was so immediate that one studio session yielded three songs, all of which they eventually released.

Bruses on Rosalía, vulnerability and redefining success

The Mexican singer-songwriter had plenty to celebrate with three Latin Grammy nominations, but she also found time to give a hat tip to the competition. “Rosalía, it’s an honor to lose to you. I love you so much,” she joked. Beyond the playful remark, the Tijuana native reflected on the emotional journey behind her album, Desde el Coma — which took three years to complete — explaining that mental health has long been central to her songwriting, which began as a form of personal journaling before her music reached a wider audience.

“I’ve always made songs about mental health, you know? And I started making music by writing as if it were my personal diary,” she said. As her career grew, so did her understanding of what achievement really means. “Success looks different to me now. It’s really beautiful, and I think I’m a very successful woman, and that has nothing to do with musical success.”

J Noa on taking aim at the music industry

The Dominican rapper found herself in an ironic position: earning a Latin Grammy nomination in the best rap/hip hop song category for “Antisistema,” a track that openly challenges the very industry recognizing her work. Rather than targeting a particular artist, J Noa explained that the track addresses the pressures imposed on musicians from all sides: “It’s like a diss track aimed at the system, but not specifically at music. It’s about the industry in general, the public, the listeners who make demands — everyone.”

What surprised her most was that the song’s confrontational message had earned such prestigious recognition. “I was really surprised that the nomination came from a song taking shots at the industry,” she said, adding that it was inspired by the desire to express “the things that we artists are always keeping quiet about.”

Francisca Valenzuela on the beautiful and brutal realities of motherhood

For Chilean singer-songwriter Francisca Valenzuela, motherhood became the inspiration for “Bugambilia,” her Latin Grammy-nominated alternative song. Written during her first postpartum experience, the track captures the emotional extremes of welcoming a child, including feelings that are often left out of the conversation. “It’s a song about the revolution that happens in that state of new motherhood, of postpartum,” she explained. “It talks about how dark it can be, because it’s not all rosy.”

While the song celebrates the love and wonder of becoming a mother, it also explores the pressure to keep going when everything feels overwhelming. Valenzuela described it as an attempt to portray a moment that is both “beautiful and brutal,” touching on “feeling inadequate, feeling like you’re collapsing under the pressure of having to perform.”

Gerardo Coronel on the $1,500 cure for heartbreak

Mexican singer-songwriter Gerardo Coronel has a rather unconventional prescription for getting over a breakup. His song “Una de 1500” draws on a familiar expression in Mexican street slang, which he uses to suggest that sometimes a little spending can help ease the pain of a failed romance. “When someone does something to you, when a relationship ends in a way you didn’t expect, sometimes you need something worth 1,500 pesos (roughly $80 USD) to help you forget or get over that trauma,” he explained.

The possibilities, according to Coronel, are practically endless — including “a psychologist who charges 1,500 pesos, a night of drinking that costs you 1,500 pesos, a little outing for 1,500 pesos, or whatever you can imagine for 1,500 pesos.” His conclusion? “One of 1,500 is very necessary to heal your sorrows.”

Milo J on his least commercial album becoming his most commercially successful

Argentine artist Milo J took a creative gamble with La Vida Era Más Corta , an album he initially considered one of his least commercially oriented projects. Rather than chasing a particular sound or audience, he focused on making something that felt authentic to him, even if it meant taking an unexpected direction. “In a way, I thought of it as a less personal album, because it’s somehow my least personal album, but perhaps the one that feels most like mine,” he explained, describing the freedom of releasing music primarily for himself and whoever wanted to listen.

The result, however, surprised him: The project connected with listeners across generations, and became one of his most commercially successful releases. “So it’s my least commercial album, but also my most commercial at the same time,” he reflected, calling its release perhaps the biggest gamble of his career. For this work, Milo earned six Latin Grammy nominations, including for album of the year.

Ovy on the Drums on why business can ruin a collaboration

Colombian hitmaker Ovy on the Drums believes some of the best musical partnerships happen when personal chemistry comes before business considerations. Discussing “Yo y Tú,” his Latin Grammy-nominated collaboration with Quevedo, the producer recalled how the song began with an initial idea developed alongside Beéle, before he shared it with the Spanish artist during a summer trip to Spain.

Quevedo immediately connected with the track, and the collaboration unfolded without complications. “It was a very natural collaboration, very easy, very fluid,” Ovy said. For him, that spontaneity makes all the difference. “When things happen that way, the music comes with a beautiful energy. Because there are songs where business gets in the way and ruins the energy.” In this case, he said, everything came together perfectly, ultimately leading to a Latin Grammy nomination.

Fonseca on fulfilling a dream with Rubén Blades

Colombian singer-songwriter Fonseca fulfilled a lifelong ambition when he joined forces with salsa legend Rubén Blades for a song addressing the experiences of migrants around the world. “Recording with maestro Rubén Blades is a dream come true. I grew up with his music, and I admire him deeply,” Fonseca said.

As the composition took shape, he realized that its message of solidarity with people pursuing their dreams far from home made Blades an ideal collaborator. After reaching out to the Panamanian icon, Fonseca was delighted by his response. “Fortunately, from the very beginning, he connected with it,” he recalled.
